name: Nehemiah

facts.author: Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes and later governor of Judah, who tells most of the story in his own words (1:1). Ezra and Nehemiah were first counted as one book, and Jewish tradition also links Ezra with it.
facts.audience: The Jews in Jerusalem and Judah after the return from exile

about: Nehemiah serves as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes in the palace at Shushan. When he hears that the wall of Jerusalem is broken down and its gates burned, he weeps, fasts and prays (1:4). The king gives him leave and letters to go and rebuild the city.

In Jerusalem Nehemiah encourages the people, and each family repairs a part of the wall. Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem mock, threaten and plot, and some Jews are oppressing their poor brothers, but Nehemiah prays, sets guards and deals with every problem. The wall is finished in only fifty-two days (6:15).

Then Ezra reads the law of God to all the people, and the Levites explain its meaning (8:8). The people weep, then rejoice and keep the feast of tabernacles. They confess their sins and make a covenant to obey God. Later Nehemiah returns from the king's court and corrects those who had broken that promise (13:6-7).

themes.title: Prayer and work together
themes.text: Nehemiah prays often, even in a moment before the king (2:4), and he also plans, builds and keeps watch.

themes.title: Courage against opposition
themes.text: Mockery, threats and lies do not stop the work, because the people trust that God will fight for them (4:20).

themes.title: The joy of the LORD
themes.text: When the law is read, the people are told not to mourn, for the joy of the LORD is their strength (8:10).

themes.title: A faithful leader
themes.text: Nehemiah refuses the governor's food allowance, cares for the poor and works beside the people (5:14-18).

themes.title: Keeping the covenant
themes.text: God's people are to keep His Sabbath, support His house and stay faithful to Him alone.
